title: Level Editor progress + Baked lightmaps for my custom AI-assisted game engine
author: Sencha-Games
selftext: I've got a "Face Carve" tool, which allows me to make doorways in seconds, and with clean edge loop topology. The overall UX has also been massively improved. Yes, I'm using Quake textures for testing, lol.

replies.author: Sencha-Games
replies.body:
I'm frustrated with general purpose engines, because when i was growing up a "game engine" came with opinions on how a game was played and authored. 

Unity and Godot will have you reinvent the wheel for every project, writing tons of boilerplate and leaving you wondering if you're even writing it the way the engine really wants you to.

My game engine is made with 3D action adventure games in mind. Specifically, Metroidvanias and Survival Horror. The authoring tools and (future) provided gameplay frameworks intend to accelerate the development and testing of those kinds of games. Right now, what differentiates the engine on a technical level is policy-based level streaming.   
  
The level editor makes it easy to partition spaces, splitting your world up into "zones" which are loaded in/out based on proximity, memory budget, and gameplay tags defined by the authors. This also compiles to a graph, which is visible from the editor so you can see the world's topology, and in the future we'll allow mutable world state which would affect the topology of your world. I think this will be useful for cool things like off-screen stalker AI, NPC schedules such as those seen in Majora's Mask, and communicating worldspace accessibility with the player!

To answer your first questions:

I've been working on this for about 5-6 months, scrapped a ton of ideas and eventually converged on ECS + Vulkan for the lower level engine core. It's mostly been built by Claude Opus, with GPT Codex filling in for some tasks. Lately, 5.6 Sol and Fable have been tremendously helpful with refactors and implementing features that have little tolerance for error margins. 

The language is C++20, favoring data oriented design and featuring minimal inheritance, almost zero in hot paths.

comments.author: Maxwell10206
comments.body: This is really cool! And I do agree with your comment about general purpose engines kind of suck with no opinion and to add to it they are very bloaty and sometimes feel like more work than they should be. I think the future will be more opinionated specific niche game engines. that are actually useful when making a game for that particular niche or design or what ever the category may be. I think the big general purpose generic game engines days are numbered. not now, but like in 10 years I doubt Unity, Unreal and sadly to say maybe even Godot will be a thing. or at least not in their current form and design..

replies.author: Sencha-Games
replies.body: My perfect utopia is that with the rise of AI, most game developers will be moving away from general purpose game engines and instead either make simpler games from scratch, or fork existing open source engines like idTech, OpenMW, or Sencha, and modify them to suit the needs of their projects.

replies.author: Sencha-Games
replies.body:
Dude I'm gonna rant, but level design has been the #1 blocker for every single 3D game I've worked on. 

I am not a fan of making a long list of "modular" pieces and running them through the asset pipeline before I'm even allowed to start making my levels. 

* SM\_Wall\_4x4
* SM\_Wall\_4x2
* SM\_Corner\_Inner\_4x4
* SM\_Corner\_Outer\_4x4
* SM\_Floor\_4x4
* SM\_Floor\_2x2
* SM\_Doorway\_4x4

Oh, I want this room to have a slightly elevated platform with a ramp leading up to it. Let me open up Blender, make 4 more models, UV map all of them perfectly so they align on a grid, set their origins to the corner (btw my level editor has a button that does this in one click), export them, import them all and point their materials back to my project's, and generate colliders for them!

I don't think I mentioned this in my other comments, but the level editor for my engine also has support for instancing, meaning that you can create "modular" kits in the same environment that you do level design in. In the future, I'll even add tools that turn this into a proper workflow.

replies.author: GoodguyGastly
replies.body:
You're speaking my language!! 😭

My current game I'm set to release on Steam is built in UE5 and I've been using a 3rd party plugin called Scythe. It's essentially trenchboom/forge. It's made my life sort of easier but still takes me forever to make something I'm kind of happy with. Anyways, that's all to say that my game has been massively delayed because of this roadblock because even though I've done all the mechanics I never thought level design was going to be the thing that destroyed me mentally. 

So that's why I've been distracting myself with building prototypes in Godot but ran into the same issues. Why do I crave the modular and proc-gen dungeons when I lack the fortitude to craft them? 😂

replies.author: Sencha-Games
replies.body:
I used Claude Code and GPT Codex!

I started off the engine by prioritizing unit tests and logging. This gives the AI agents enough feedback to rapidly (and I  mean RAPIDLY) iterate on a new feature until it converges on the version that finally works. I don't think i could have had Opus 4.7 write a full Vulkan renderer if not for this.   
  
I used textures from Quake to build this test level! The list of library dependencies is pretty short.
